entry.title: Building an MCP Server with SAP CAP on SAP BTP: AI Assistant for SAP S/4HANA (Part 1 of 2)
entry.content:
Introduction

An earlier post, Connecting SAP S/4HANA to AI with MCP and SAP BTP, described a small MCP server in Python that let an AI assistant read SAP S/4HANA data through OData. The approach worked, but every part of it was custom code: a custom login check, custom logging and a custom deployment.

This two-part series rebuilds the same assistant the SAP way, with the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) on SAP BTP. The result is one CAP application that answers questions about SAP S/4HANA data, both through an MCP endpoint for AI tools and through standard OData.

  • Part 1 (this post): the architecture, the CAP project file by file, connecting to S/4HANA, the MCP endpoint, login with the user's own token, and deployment.
  • Part 2: securing the application and adding AI-powered SAP Basis monitoring over RFC.

This post is for SAP Basis, BTP and integration people who know S/4HANA and want a working pattern for connecting AI to it. Full-time development experience is not required; the places where SAP Basis knowledge matters are highlighted along the way.

Why SAP CAP instead of a hand-written MCP server

CAP provides, out of the box, the capabilities that previously had to be built by hand, in a form that other SAP teams recognise and can support.

Topic Hand-written Python server SAP CAP application

LoginCustom API key checkXSUAA login and roles, checked by CAP for every request
Who may do whatOne key for everyoneRole collections in the BTP cockpit, e.g. User
Connecting to S/4HANACustom HTTP calls and credentialsCAP remote services through a BTP destination and the Cloud Connector
Audit trailPrint statements@cap-js/audit-logging, SAP's standard plugin (Part 2)
Personal dataNot described@PersonalData annotations in the CDS model
Deploymentcf push per appOne MTA archive: mbt build and cf deploy

The tools themselves stay almost the same. The difference is everything around them: login, roles, connectivity, logging and deployment now follow the SAP standard.

Architecture

Users only ever open the approuter. It handles the login and passes the user's token to the chat website, which calls the CAP app with that same token. The CAP app reaches S/4HANA through the BTP destination and the Cloud Connector. Nothing stores business data on the way.

Prerequisites

  • SAP BTP subaccount with Cloud Foundry enabled, and entitlements for Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA), Destination and Connectivity.
  • SAP Cloud Connector connected to the subaccount, exposing the S/4HANA Gateway (/sap/opu/odata/).
  • A BTP destination of type HTTP to S/4HANA through the Cloud Connector (ProxyType: OnPremise).
  • SAP S/4HANA with the standard OData APIs activated in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, e.g. API_BUSINESS_PARTNER and API_SALES_ORDER_SRV.
  • A technical SAP user for the destination. Read-only authorizations only; more on this in Part 2.
  • On your laptop: Node.js 22, @SAP/cds-dk (npm i -g @SAP/cds-dk), the Cloud MTA Build Tool (npm i -g mbt) and the Cloud Foundry CLI with the MultiApps plugin.

The project, file by file

The project is created with cds init and keeps CAP's standard layout. The following files make it a CAP project and are the best starting point:

sap-ai-assistant-cap/
├─ package.json          CAP dependencies and the cds configuration (remote services, auth, audit log)
├─ srv/
│  ├─ s4-service.cds     the service: entities and one function per tool, @requires: 'User'
│  ├─ s4-service.js      the handlers behind those functions
│  ├─ external/          imported SAP API definitions (cds import)
│  ├─ server.js          start-up: destination, MCP endpoint
│  ├─ mcp.js             the MCP endpoint /mcp
│  └─ sap/               the tools, the allow-list of SAP APIs, metadata reading
├─ app/
│  ├─ router/            the approuter: the only address users open (login)
│  └─ web/               the chat website
├─ xs-security.json      scopes and role collections
└─ mta.yaml              how everything is built and deployed together

The three that matter most:

  • srv/s4-service.cds declares the service: who may use it, and which functions it offers.
  • package.json, in its cds section, declares where SAP is, how login works and where audit entries go. It's configuration, not code.
  • mta.yaml puts the CAP app, the website and the approuter into one deployable archive, together with the BTP services they need.

A quick way to tell a CAP project from "Node.js code that calls SAP" is cds watch. It starts the whole service locally, with mocked login, from these files alone.

Connecting CAP to SAP S/4HANA

CAP reaches S/4HANA through a remote service that points at the BTP destination. No URL, user or password is in the code; the destination and the Cloud Connector handle all of that.

First, import the API definition of the Business Partner API (the EDMX from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub):

cds import API_BUSINESS_PARTNER.edmx --as cds

Then declare the remote services in package.json. The destination name is set at deployment, not in the code:

"cds": {
  "requires": {
    "API_BUSINESS_PARTNER": { "kind": "odata-v2", "model": "srv/external/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER" },
    "S4HANA": { "kind": "odata-v2", "credentials": { "path": "/sap/opu/odata" } }
  }
}

In srv/server.js, every remote service gets the destination from an environment variable that mta.yaml fills in:

const destination = process.env.SAP_DESTINATION
for (const conf of Object.values(cds.env.requires)) {
  if (conf?.kind === 'odata-v2') conf.credentials = { ...conf.credentials, destination }
}

The application uses two styles of access:

  • Typed CDS queries on imported APIs, e.g. a projection on A_BusinessPartner. CAP translates OData V4 options such as $filter and $select into the V2 call automatically.
  • Raw OData V2 calls for everything else: await s4.send({ method: 'GET', path: 'sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV/A_SalesOrder?$top=5' }). This lets the tools work with any allowed API without importing each one.

Two Basis details to check before investigating the code:

  1. Cloud Connector resource: the path /sap/opu/odata/ must be exposed, with "path and all sub-paths".
  2. The services must be active in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE. A service that isn't answers with a 403 or 404 that looks like an authorization problem.

Tools as CAP functions, and the MCP endpoint

Every tool exists once and is offered through two doors: as a CAP function over OData, and as an MCP tool at /mcp. Both give exactly the same answer text, because both call the same JavaScript function.

The service in srv/s4-service.cds:

@requires: 'User'
@path    : '/odata/v4/s4'
service S4Service {

  @readonly
  entity BusinessPartners as projection on bp.A_BusinessPartner {
    key BusinessPartner, BusinessPartnerFullName as Name, CreationDate
  };

  function list_sap_services(search : String)                           returns LargeString;
  function query_sap(![service] : String, entity_set : String,
                     ![filter] : String, ![select] : String, top : Integer) returns LargeString;
  function find_sap_data(question : String, top : Integer)               returns LargeString;
  function search_business_partners(name : String, top : Integer)       returns LargeString;
  function get_sales_order(sales_order : String)                         returns LargeString;
  // ... one function per tool
}

@requires: 'User' is the whole authorization check for the OData door. CAP refuses any request without a valid login (401) or without the User role (403) before any application code runs. @readonlyand the absence of any create/update function make the service read-only by design.

The MCP endpoint is a small Express route in srv/mcp.js, using the official SDK @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. It sits behind CAP's own login middleware, so the same check applies:

app.post('/mcp', ...cds.middlewares.before, requireUser,
         express.json({ limit: '1mb' }), handle)

handle creates a stateless MCP server for each request. It lists the tools (each marked readOnlyHint: true) and runs a tool by calling the same function the OData door uses. Being stateless means several app instances can serve the same chat without shared sessions.

For /mcp, cds.middlewares.before is the key line: it gives a custom route the same login, user context and audit hooks as CAP's own services.

Answering plain-English questions from SAP's own metadata

Fixed tools only answer the questions that were anticipated at design time. To go further, the assistant gets four general tools:

Tool What it does

list_sap_servicesLists the SAP APIs the assistant may use: an allow-list, cross-checked against the services that are really registered in the system (/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE)
describe_sap_serviceReads an API's $metadata: its entity sets, fields with their SAP labels, and links
query_sapReads rows with $filter, $select, $orderby and $top, with a hard limit on rows and answer size
find_sap_dataTakes one plain-English question and works out the service, entity set and filters itself

find_sap_data is the most powerful of the four. It reads every allowed service's $metadata (cached for an hour) and scores each entity set against the words in the question. It uses SAP's own descriptions and field labels, so "how many sales orders were created last month" finds A_SalesOrder and CreationDate without a single hardcoded mapping. The answer always states exactly what it queried, so a user can check it.

The project follows a strict rule: no company data, sample IDs or hardcoded values in the code. Every number, name and ID in an answer comes from SAP at the moment of the question. Adding a new standard API is a configuration change (SAP_EXTRA_SERVICES), not a code change.

Login and roles: the user's own token, no shared key

The biggest change from the Python version: there is no shared API key any more. Every request carries the signed-in user's own login token.

  1. The user opens the approuter address, the only address users ever open. The approuter sends them to the login page of the subaccount's identity provider.
  2. After login, the approuter passes the user's XSUAA token on to the chat website (forwardAuthToken: true).
  3. The website calls the CAP app's /mcp with that same token.
  4. CAP checks the token and the User role on every request, for OData and MCP alike.

The roles are defined in xs-security.json:

{
  "scopes": [{ "name": "$XSAPPNAME.User", "description": "Use the SAP assistant" }],
  "role-templates": [{ "name": "User", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.User"] }],
  "role-collections": [{
    "name": "SAP AI Assistant CAP User",
    "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.User"]
  }]
}

An administrator assigns the role collection to users in the BTP cockpit (Security → Users). Because the token belongs to a person, CAP knows who asked what, which the audit log in Part 2 builds on.

In mta.yaml, the login service's redirect-uris are also restricted to the approuter's own address. As a result, no other app on the shared cfapps domain can receive a login result meant for this one.

Important: once a role collection is assigned to users, you can't add roles to it through xs-security.json. The XSUAA service update fails with "Adding role-template-references to role collection ... is restricted". Create a new role collection with a new name instead.

Build and deploy

Everything goes to Cloud Foundry as one MTA archive. mta.yaml describes three apps and the services they use:

Module What it is Binds

...-srvThe CAP app: OData and /mcpXSUAA, Destination, Connectivity
...-webThe chat websiteXSUAA
...-routerThe approuter, the only address users openXSUAA

System-specific values are kept out of git in a small extension file, config.mtaext:

_schema-version: '3.1'
ID: sap-ai-assistant-cap.config
extends: sap-ai-assistant-cap
parameters:
  sap-destination: <your BTP destination name>
  router-host: <the host name users open>

Then build and deploy:

npm ci
mbt build
cf deploy mta_archives/sap-ai-assistant-cap_1.0.0.mtar -e config.mtaext

Finally, assign the role collection to the users in the BTP cockpit.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them:

  1. Build timeout. On a laptop, the website's build took longer than mbt's default 10 minutes, so an old archive was deployed without any warning. Fix: build-parameters: timeout: 40m on that module.
  2. Stack deprecation. Cloud Foundry warned that cflinuxfs4 is deprecated. Fix: stack: cflinuxfs5 on each module, then rebuild and redeploy (a restage alone doesn't change it).
  3. Role collections are frozen once assigned. See the login section: create a new collection rather than changing an assigned one.
  4. Duplicate downloads. When a new version of the project zip is downloaded, the browser may save it as ... (1).zip, and the old archive is easily unpacked by mistake. A quick Select-String for a new line of code before mbt build saves a lot of confusion.

The result

Users open one address, log in with their normal company account, and ask questions about SAP S/4HANA data in plain English. Every answer is read live from SAP at the moment of the question.

Key points for SAP Basis consultants:

  • One login, checked twice. The website checks the token, and the CAP app checks it again for every request. Someone who finds the CAP app's own address still can't get in without a valid token and the role.
  • Nothing stored. There's no database; every answer comes from SAP when it's asked, so there's no copy of business data in BTP.
  • Read-only by design. The service has no write functions and its entities are @readonly.

Conclusion and what's next

Rebuilding the MCP server with SAP CAP took more thought than writing a Python script, but the result is something an SAP team can own:

  • standard login and roles;
  • connectivity through the destination and the Cloud Connector;
  • one deployable archive.

The AI side, the MCP endpoint, turned out to be the smallest part. Doing it properly on BTP was the real work.

Part 2 covers what it takes to make the application safe to put in front of real users:

  • a line-by-line security review of the code, including a text pattern that could freeze the app;
  • data rules for the SAP APIs, request limits and the SAP audit log;
  • AI-powered SAP Basis monitoring over RFC, with a dashboard for SM51, SM04, SM58 and SM37.

Thanks for reading. If you've built something similar with CAP and MCP, or have questions about any of the steps, feel free to share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: "Is there a CDS view for that table?" Answered in SAP Datasphere, no S/4HANA user needed
entry.content:
The situation (you have probably been here)

SAP Datasphere is up and running. The connection to SAP S/4HANA is green. The first replication flow is happily moving data. Everything is perfect, except for one small detail: your own S/4HANA user. It has been "requested". The ticket has been "in progress" for three weeks. It has seen more status changes than some of your sales orders. 🙃

And of course, this is exactly the moment someone asks: "We need table X with columns A, B and C. Is there a CDS view we can replicate? Ideally with delta?"

Without an S/4HANA user you have no SE11 where-used list, no ADT and no View Browser. What you do have is the source browser of the replication flow, which searches names and descriptions. It cannot tell you which columns a view contains. It also keeps quiet about filters a view applies. That leaves you with educated guessing, or with asking a colleague at the customer for screenshots, again.

In my case the table was BUT050 (business partner relationships). Instead of guessing, I built a small metadata model that only needs the Datasphere connection that is already there. It has since become a self-service tool for the developers on the project.

What already exists

Credit where it is due. There are good tools for this question:

  • In the S/4HANA system: the where-used list in SE11, the SQL Dependency Analyzer in ADT, the View Browser app, or SE16 on DD26S plus DDLDEPENDENCY. All of them need an S/4HANA user.
  • I_DataExtractionEnabledView (SQL view IXTRCTNENBLDVW, available since S/4HANA 2020) lists the CDS views that are enabled for extraction. See CDS Views Enabled for Data Extraction and KBA 3472575.
  • Top-down analysis in Datasphere: McCoy & Partners describe how to replicate the CDS view stack (DDCDS_BOE_VIEWSTACK_INFO_UNION) and resolve the dependencies of a given CDS view in Datasphere: Gaining additional insights into technical details of CDS views.
  • Field-level mapping without any system: the community SAP Table to CDS Mapper (Project Kernseife) maps table fields to CDS elements for a standard S/4HANA 2025 system, including C1 release information.

What I was missing was the bottom-up direction (table → views), answered for the actual system, including custom Z views:

  1. Which CDS views are built on this table, and which of them are extraction-enabled, released and CDC-capable?
  2. Which view column comes from which table field?
  3. Does the view apply a WHERE filter?

The idea: six DDIC objects as remote tables

Everything you need is in the ABAP Dictionary. Datasphere can read it through the S/4HANA on-premise connection as remote tables (container ABAPTABLES). Replicate them as snapshots once a week, for example with a task chain. That is enough, because metadata only changes with transports.

DDIC object Content Used for

DD26SView → base table / base viewView lineage
DD27SView field → base table fieldField lineage
DD28SConditions of a view (WHERE and join conditions)Filters
DDLDEPENDENCYDDL source ↔ CDS entity (OBJECTTYPE = 'STOB') ↔ generated SQL view ('VIEW')Name resolution
DDDDLSRCTDescription of DDL sourcesDescriptions
IXTRCTNENBLDVWSQL view of I_DataExtractionEnabledViewExtraction, release and CDC flags

A detail that surprised me: the ABAPTABLES container does not only offer tables. It also offers the generated SQL views of CDS views. That is how I_DataExtractionEnabledView ends up in Datasphere without a replication flow. In our system each of the six objects replicated in under a minute (5 to 51 seconds).

Option 1: Quick & dirty, one SQL view

If you just want an answer today, a single SQL view does the job. Create it in the space that holds the six remote tables, paste the statement and open the data preview. Change BUT050 in the last line to your table. The second condition keeps CDS views only. Remove it if you also want to see classic DDIC views.

It returns one row per table field and CDS view column, with the CDS view name, its description, the three flags and the view's filter. It follows views up to four levels above the table. Each level is one more UNION ALL block, so extending it is copy and paste.

SELECT l."BaseTable",
	l."BaseField",
	l."Level",
	e."OBJECTNAME" AS "CdsEntity",
	l."SqlView",
	l."CdsField",
	t."DDTEXT" AS "Description",
	CASE WHEN x."DATAEXTRACTIONVIEWNAME" IS NULL THEN '' ELSE 'X' END AS "IsExtractionEnabled",
	x."ISSAPRELEASEDVIEW" AS "IsSapReleased",
	x."DELTACHGDATACAPTUREISSUPPORTED" AS "IsCdcSupported",
	flt."Filter"
FROM (
	SELECT p."BaseTable", p."BaseField", p."SqlView", p."CdsField", MIN(p."Level") AS "Level"
	FROM (
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 1 AS "Level", f1."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f1."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		UNION ALL
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 2 AS "Level", f2."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f2."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f2 ON f2."TABNAME" = f1."VIEWNAME" AND f2."FIELDNAME" = f1."VIEWFIELD" AND f2."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f2."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		UNION ALL
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 3 AS "Level", f3."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f3."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f2 ON f2."TABNAME" = f1."VIEWNAME" AND f2."FIELDNAME" = f1."VIEWFIELD" AND f2."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f2."AS4VERS" = '0000'
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f3 ON f3."TABNAME" = f2."VIEWNAME" AND f3."FIELDNAME" = f2."VIEWFIELD" AND f3."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f3."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		UNION ALL
		SELECT f1."TABNAME" AS "BaseTable", f1."FIELDNAME" AS "BaseField", 4 AS "Level", f4."VIEWNAME" AS "SqlView", f4."VIEWFIELD" AS "CdsField"
		FROM "DD27S" AS f1
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f2 ON f2."TABNAME" = f1."VIEWNAME" AND f2."FIELDNAME" = f1."VIEWFIELD" AND f2."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f2."AS4VERS" = '0000'
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f3 ON f3."TABNAME" = f2."VIEWNAME" AND f3."FIELDNAME" = f2."VIEWFIELD" AND f3."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f3."AS4VERS" = '0000'
			INNER JOIN "DD27S" AS f4 ON f4."TABNAME" = f3."VIEWNAME" AND f4."FIELDNAME" = f3."VIEWFIELD" AND f4."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f4."AS4VERS" = '0000'
		WHERE f1."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND f1."AS4VERS" = '0000'
	) AS p
	GROUP BY p."BaseTable", p."BaseField", p."SqlView", p."CdsField"
) AS l
	LEFT JOIN "DDLDEPENDENCY" AS w ON w."OBJECTNAME" = l."SqlView" AND w."OBJECTTYPE" = 'VIEW' AND w."STATE" = 'A'
	LEFT JOIN "DDLDEPENDENCY" AS e ON e."DDLNAME" = w."DDLNAME" AND e."OBJECTTYPE" = 'STOB' AND e."STATE" = 'A'
	LEFT JOIN "DDDDLSRCT" AS t ON t."DDLNAME" = w."DDLNAME" AND t."DDLANGUAGE" = 'E' AND t."AS4LOCAL" = 'A'
	LEFT JOIN "IXTRCTNENBLDVW" AS x ON UPPER(x."DATAEXTRACTIONVIEWNAME") = e."OBJECTNAME"
	LEFT JOIN (
		SELECT c."CONDNAME", STRING_AGG(TRIM(COALESCE(c."NEGATION", '') || ' ' || c."TABNAME" || '.' || c."FIELDNAME" || ' ' || c."OPERATOR" || ' ' || c."CONSTANTS" || ' ' || COALESCE(c."AND_OR", '')), ' ' ORDER BY c."POSITION") AS "Filter"
		FROM "DD28S" AS c
		WHERE c."AS4LOCAL" = 'A' AND c."AS4VERS" = '0000' AND COALESCE(c."CONSTANTS", '') NOT LIKE '&$SESSION%'
		GROUP BY c."CONDNAME"
	) AS flt ON flt."CONDNAME" = l."SqlView"
WHERE l."BaseTable" = 'BUT050' AND e."OBJECTNAME" IS NOT NULL

How to read the result:

  • Table → views: look at the distinct CdsEntity values, ideally with IsExtractionEnabled = 'X'.
  • Columns: BaseField is the table field, CdsField the view column. In a replication flow the column shows up in CamelCase (RELATIONSHIPCATEGORY → RelationshipCategory).
  • Filter: the conditions of the view as text. The client condition (CLIENT EQ &$SESSION.CLIENT) that every client-dependent view carries is hidden. Lines starting with JL are join conditions, everything else filters rows.

Filtered on I_BPCONTACT: extraction-enabled, released, CDC-capable, and filtered on RELTYP EQ 'BUR001'. The last row shows a level-2 view (I_BPCONTACTTOFUNCANDDEPT) whose join to BUT051 appears as a JL ... JR ... line.

A word of honesty: this is a quick & dirty solution, not a sustainable architecture. It is one big statement, it checks filters only on the view itself and not on the views further down the path, and anyone who edits it in a hurry will regret it later. For a one-off answer it is perfect. If you want to offer it to a team for the long run, read on.

Option 2: A small layered model

For a permanent self-service tool I split the logic into reusable views. The names below are deliberately neutral, so adapt them to your naming convention.

View Purpose

DDIC_VIEW_EDGEView → base object from DD26S (active version), CDS entity names mapped to SQL view names, CAST helper tables DDDDL*TYPES filtered out
DDIC_VIEW_FIELDView fields with their origin from DD27S
DDIC_VIEW_CONDITIONWHERE and join conditions from DD28S as readable text
CDS_OBJECTDDL source → CDS entity → SQL view
CDS_EXTRACTION_ENABLEDExtraction-enabled views with release and CDC flags (joined via UPPER, see below)
CDS_TABLE_LINEAGETable → CDS view, shortest level, all flags, example path
CDS_FIELD_LINEAGETable field → CDS view field, all flags
CDS_VIEW_FILTERFilters per CDS view

Datasphere SQL views support neither WITH nor recursive queries. The lineage views therefore use the same trick as option 1: an unrolled UNION ALL, where level k is a k-fold self-join of the edge view. Six levels covered every case I looked at:

SELECT e1."BaseName" AS "BaseTable",
	2 AS "Level",
	e2."ViewName" AS "ViewName",
	e1."BaseName" || ' > ' || e1."ViewName" || ' > ' || e2."ViewName" AS "Path"
FROM "DDIC_VIEW_EDGE" AS e1
	INNER JOIN "DDIC_VIEW_EDGE" AS e2 ON e2."BaseNode" = e1."ViewName"

A filter on BaseTable is pushed down into level 1, so a query for one table comes back within seconds, even though the views cover the whole dictionary.

Writing six levels by hand is no fun, so I generate the views with a small Python script. It renders every expression twice, as SQL text and as query CSN, and deploys the views via the Datasphere CLI. One CLI pitfall: a SQL view created via CLI without a query CSN deploys "successfully" but returns no rows.

Walking through BUT050

Step 1: Which views are built on the table, and which are extraction-enabled?

Selected candidates on BUT050. Only I_BPCONTACT is extraction-enabled, released and CDC-capable. I_BPRELATIONSHIP_2 exists, but is not enabled for extraction.

Step 2: Which view contains PARTNER1, PARTNER2 and RELTYP?

Three candidate views deliver the fields. Only I_BPCONTACT is extraction-enabled.

Step 3: Does that view filter rows?

And there is the catch: BUT050.RELTYP EQ 'BUR001'.

So the only extraction-enabled view with all three columns delivers contact person relationships only. Our requirement was a customer-specific relationship category, which this view will never return. Without the model we would have found that out after the first load, most likely as "why are so many relationships missing?".

The result for this case: a custom view on I_BPRELATIONSHIP_2 with @analytics.dataExtraction.enabled: true (and CDC), plus a remote table snapshot on BUT050 until then.

Lessons learned, so you don't have to

  1. Upper and lower case. IXTRCTNENBLDVW returns entity names as written in the DDL source, in CamelCase (I_BPContact). DDLDEPENDENCY, DD26S and DD27S use upper case. Without UPPER() in the join, only views whose DDL name is written in upper case match, and every VDM standard view drops out. The nasty part: the result still looks plausible.
  2. Keep your hands off DDHEADANNO. The CDS header annotation table (with a 1,300-character VALUE column) took down our Data Provisioning Agent twice. After about 6.5 minutes the load failed, and from then on every remote table replication in the tenant reported "data provisioning agent is unavailable" until the agent was reconnected. Two out of two is a big enough sample for me. IXTRCTNENBLDVW already provides the extraction and CDC information in condensed form. Replicate any new dictionary table on its own once before you add it to a task chain.
  3. DD28S does contain CDS filters, plus some noise. For CDS SQL views, DD28S contains the WHERE conditions and, for views with joins, the join conditions (marked JL/JR). Every client-dependent view also has a line CLIENT EQ &$SESSION.CLIENT, which you want to hide. AND_OR belongs at the end of a line, not at the start.
  4. Column names. DD27S.VIEWFIELD is upper case (RELATIONSHIPCATEGORY). In the replication flow the same column is called RelationshipCategory.
  5. Coverage check. In our system IXTRCTNENBLDVW lists 5,146 extraction-enabled views. 4,062 of them have a generated SQL view, and all 4,062 were found in DD26S. The remaining 1,084 are view entities (define view entity) without an SQL view, and those are invisible to DD26S, DD27S and DD28S.

Limitations

  • View entities without an SQL view are missing (see lesson 5). For those, the Kernseife mapper is a good cross-check, and DDCDS_BOE_VIEWSTACK_INFO_UNION might close the gap. I have not tested that yet.
  • Filters are only the conditions stored in the dictionary (WHERE and join conditions). Parameters and DCL authorizations are not covered. A quick count after the first load is still a good idea.
  • Release and system state: tested on one S/4HANA on-premise system. Community posts report that I_DataExtractionEnabledView does not necessarily expose every entry known to ODP. I did not verify that.
  • Authorizations: you do not need your own S/4HANA user, but the technical user behind the Datasphere connection must be allowed to read the dictionary tables.

Conclusion

Six dictionary tables, one SQL view (or a handful, if you like it tidy) and a weekly task chain turn "Is there a CDS view for that?" from a guessing game into a three-minute check. It also works for developers who have no S/4HANA access at all. At our customer it now lives on a Confluence page with copy-and-paste queries. My S/4HANA user did arrive in the end, by the way. I barely needed it for this.

I'm curious which table triggers the question in your project, and whether anyone has combined this with DDCDS_BOE_VIEWSTACK_INFO_UNION to cover view entities as well.

Disclosure: This blog post was written with the support of generative AI. The approach, the SQL and all results shown were built, tested and reviewed by me in a SAP Datasphere and SAP S/4HANA system.

entry.title: Model company for SAP cloud solutions: Helping consultants make better Fit-to-Standard decisions
entry.content:
Part 3 of the blog series on model company for SAP cloud solutions

 

Introduction

 

Anyone who has prepared a Fit-to-Standard workshop knows how much work goes into getting ready. You need a system that runs, a relevant business scenario, and data that make sense to the customer. Without these, it is easy for the discussion to stay at the level of slides and assumptions.

Model company for SAP cloud solutions can help. It provides preconfigured reference content for available industries and lines of business. Once this content is deployed, consultants can demonstrate working SAP S/4HANA processes, supported by process flow diagrams and test materials. This makes it easier to prepare workshops around real business questions.

Part 1 of this series explained what a model company is. Part 2 looked at it from an architect’s perspective. This article focuses on what consultants can do with it: prepare workshops, assess how standard processes meet customer needs, identify justified requirements and turn business decisions into clear next steps for implementation.

 

The Consultant’s Challenge: From Preparation to Value

 

Before a workshop can start, someone must get the groundwork right: set up relevant processes, prepare master and transactional data, test the scenarios, and make sure everything runs smoothly. Much of this work is repeated from one project to the next. If too much time goes into setup, there is less time to discuss what the business needs.

Model company can reduce this effort by providing a preconfigured reference system. It does not remove the need to be prepared.  Consultants still need to check whether the right industry and country scope is available, whether the environment is ready, and which of the delivered scenarios are most relevant to the business discussions. The difference is that they can spend more time deciding what to validate with the business and less time setting up examples.

 

What consultants can use in model company

 

Depending on the available industry and line-of-business content, consultants can use:

  • Working process scenarios: Preconfigured end-to-end business processes that can be run and demonstrated in the reference environment.
  • Business data: Sample master data that enables consultants to run business scenarios, create transactions, and experience how the processes work in practice.
  • Process and project materials: Process flow diagrams available for download or as SAP Signavio process models for further adaption, complemented by SAP Cloud ALM scope materials, for those using SAP Cloud ALM, to support workshops and follow-up activities.
  • Test materials: Available test scripts to guide scenario execution and support testing activities in later project phases. Automated tests are not available for every scenario.

Not every industry has the same content. Check out the current industry and line-of-business dashboard, linked from Part 1, before planning a workshop around a specific scenario.

 

Show & tell in practice: from demonstration to decision

 

A Show & Tell session makes Fit-to-Standard tangible. In a procure-to-pay workshop, the consultant checks the relevant model company scenario, reference environment and data before guiding business users through the live process e.g.:

  • Create a purchase requisition
  • Turn it into a purchase order
  • Receive the goods
  • Process the supplier invoice
  • Make the payment

The goal is to discuss business needs alongside the demonstration and walkthrough. The consultant pauses at key steps, such as purchase order approval, to explore the customer's controls within the working process. This gives business users a real sense of their processes in practice and the ability to link visuals with concepts, ultimately speeding up decision-making and reducing the risk of future changes.

Figure 1. A live procure-to-pay process anchors the Show & Tell discussion.

A purchasing manager says, “We need three approval levels before a purchase order can be released.” The consultant asks why. Is this a legal or internal control requirement? What risk does it address? Or is it an inherited practice?

Compare the requirements with the live process and any supported configuration options. The discussion may lead to three outcomes:

  • Standard process meets the need: No change is required.
  • Configuration can meet the need: A supported configuration option should be checked against the customer’s requirements.
  • Further assessment is needed: A justified exception needs a clear reason, an owner, and a decision once the impact is understood.

For example, the team could confirm standard purchase order creation, ask the consultant to verify supported approval configuration, and involve the architect if an external approval is justified. Give each open item to the owner and take the next step. This prevents every difference from the current system from becoming a deviation. 

 

Before, during and after the workshop

Before: prepare the right questions

Confirm the required industry content and access to a provisioned model company reference environment. Check business roles and sample data, rehearse the selected scenario from end to end, and agree which decisions the Show & Tell must support. For scope and request instructions, see SAP Note 3631601.

During: work through the business decisions

Introduce the business context, then run the process live and pause where important decisions arise. Ask whether each step supports what the business needs. Separate what fits, what may need configuration and what needs further assessment. For open items, record why they matter, who will follow up, and when a decision is expected. SAP Cloud ALM can support this by capturing requirements, decisions and follow-up activities directly against the model company scope elements already available in the tool. Your role is to guide a useful discussion, not simply write down every difference.

After: turn decisions into next steps

Summarize the agreed process scope, open configuration questions, justified requirements, and any impact on testing. If the project uses SAP Signavio and SAP Cloud ALM, their process models and project materials can help teams record and track the outcomes. With model company scope elements already available in SAP Cloud ALM, teams can build on this foundation to capture workshop decisions, requirements, and follow-up activities.

A future deep-dive article will show how to access and prepare a model company environment, select a scenario and run a Show & Tell session from setup through follow-up.

 

How model company supports SAP Activate

 

Model company is especially useful when preparing workshops and validating processes during Explore. Its content and supporting materials can also help in later phases. SAP Activate has six phases: Discover, Prepare, Explore, Realize, Deploy and Run. The illustration below focuses on the work consultants do from Prepare onward and groups Deploy and Run together.

One important point: model company serve as a reference for the project. It is not necessarily the environment used to build or run the customer’s solution.

  • Prepare: Access or set up the available model company reference, then choose the processes, data and materials needed for the customer’s workshops.
  • Explore: Demonstrate live end-to-end scenarios, check whether they meet business needs and document the decisions and justify requirements that will guide the implementation.
  • Realize: Apply the agreed decisions in the customer implementation environment. Use relevant reference content and available test materials to support configuration, extensions, and testing.
  • Deploy and Run: Use the process knowledge, documented decisions and applicable test assets to help with go-live preparation, handover and later improvements.

Figure 2. How consultants can use model company during the implementation journey (simplified view).

Keeping the core clean in day-to-day work

 

Clean core is not only an architecture topic. Consultants influence it whenever they accept a requirement, choose a configuration option or propose an extension. Model company offers a reference aligned with clean-core principles, but the customer solution still needs to be designed and built accordingly.

First, check whether the business needs can be met through the standard process or supported configuration. If an extension is justified, discuss the options with the architect and follow the approach supported for the customer solution. This may include key-user, developer/on-stack or side-by-side extensibility, using released interfaces and APIs where required. Record why the decision was made and how it will be tested, so the teams who take over can understand and maintain it.

 

Working with architects

 

Consultants and architects need to work from the same process decisions, but their responsibilities are different. Architects set the overall design and technical boundaries. Consultants work with business users to confirm which processes fit and turn those decisions into configuration, requirements and tests for the customer environment. Keeping process models and decisions up to date helps both roles stay aligned.

 

Conclusion: better decisions, not just faster preparation

 

For consultants, the biggest advantage is not simply having access to a preconfigured system. It can show a real process, question assumptions, and distinguish genuine business requirements from habits carried over from the previous system.
